query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Doping the high‐entropy alloy (HEA) with a small volume fraction of a carbide precursor (e.g., vanadium carbide) will enable shear‐activated in situ decomposition during sliding to supply carbon and vanadium that, in the presence of ambient oxygen, form a composite amorphous carbon/vanadium oxide tribofilm. This tribofilm reduces both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate over a broad temperature range without relying on external lubricants or solvents.
generation.material_initial_state: A self‐lubricating, high‐entropy alloy formulated without pre‐existing discrete lubricating phases.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled, low-volume fraction (e.g., 2–5 wt%) of vanadium carbide (VC) into the HEA during processing.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests in ambient air across a wide service-temperature range (e.g., room temperature up to 800 °C) where oxygen is available for the reactive process.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a nanostructured composite tribofilm composed of amorphous carbon interspersed with fine vanadium oxide crystallites, generated in situ by the decomposition of VC during shear.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, the mechanical stress induces the decomposition of the finely dispersed VC phase. The released carbon immediately reorganizes into an amorphous lubricious layer while the liberated vanadium oxidizes with ambient oxygen to form a low-shear V-oxide. Together, these phases create a continuous, self-healing protective tribofilm that reduces metal-to-metal contact and lowers friction and wear even at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an identical HEA without the VC additive, the treated alloy should exhibit a reduction in the coefficient of friction by approximately 25–30% and a one-order-of-magnitude lower wear rate, maintained across the designated temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated self-lubricating HEA that relies solely on its intrinsic microstructure for tribological performance (without additive-induced tribofilm formation).
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the tribofilm is expected when ambient oxygen is present (i.e., in air) and may not be realized in oxygen-deprived or inert environments. Additionally, the optimal VC concentration must avoid excessive carbide content that could embrittle the alloy.
generation.uncertainty: While reactive wear protection mechanisms (as reported in the TiNbZr-Ag alloy study, PMC8448869) and tribocatalytic formation of lubricious carbon layers in 2D HEA systems (PMC12019924) support the individual roles of reactive oxide formation and tribocatalysis, combining them through a carbide precursor in a bulk HEA is untested. The scale of carbon/oxide generation and its uniformity across a wide temperature range remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples – one group of HEAs doped with 2–5 wt% vanadium carbide and an otherwise identical control group without VC. Process both via the same route to ensure comparable microstructures. Conduct ball-on-disc sliding tests in ambient air over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, systematically measuring the coefficient of friction and wear rates. Analyze the worn surfaces using SEM, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS to detect the presence and composition of any in situ-formed tribofilms.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) as a function of temperature and sliding distance
Wear volume/rate from wear track profiling
Surface chemical composition and phase identification from Raman spectroscopy and XPS
Microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS) of the worn surfaces to verify tribofilm formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the VC-doped HEA does not form a continuous, carbon/vanadium oxide-rich tribofilm (as verified by surface analyses) and fails to show a statistically significant reduction in both the COF and wear rate (by at least ~25% and one order-of-magnitude respectively) compared to the control across the temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of vanadium changed the microstructure of the alloy. The microstructure of the Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy is two phase, consisting of a mixture of fcc and bcc phases with slightly different chemical compositions, mainly with different proportions of aluminum and chromium. On the other hand, the modification of the alloy with the addition of vanadium resulted in homogenization of the structure. The addition of vanadium increased the hardness of the material by about 33%. The proposed modification also increased the wear resistance of the alloy—the wear value decreased by 73%. Notably, the wear mechanism has also changed. In the case of the unmodified Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy, the wear was of mixed adhesive–abrasive nature with the formation of a secondary layer. On the other hand, the Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5 alloy was dominated by abrasive wear with the presence of oxide wear products lifted from the friction zone.

The (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 powder is combined with distilled water at a concentration of 1.5g L−1. This water‐based lubricant solution was sonicated for thorough mixing (≈9 h sonication time) and spray coated uniformly onto the steel disk for ball‐on‐disk friction experiments across all loads from 1 N to 9 N. In summary, we propose a strategy to design wear-resistant alloys through in-situ formation of strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces during wear, a process which we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. A representative bcc structured (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy was developed, which yields a two orders of magnitude lower wear rate than the reference TiNbZr alloy. Upon wear in ambient air, the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy forms an in-situ 400-nm-thick amorphous-crystalline nanocomposite surface layer, through reaction with the environmental O, comprising an amorphous Ti17Nb13Zr13Fe2O55 matrix containing ~10-nm-sized Ag nanocrystals.
